column3: Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls Abigail Nabal’s wife; BSB calls her his widow.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew leaves the questioner unnamed and says he asked why Abner had “gone in to” the concubine; BSB names Ish-bosheth and says “sleep with.”
The Hebrew twice uses “today”; BSB has “All this time” and “now.” It calls Ish-bosheth’s statement “words,” rendered “accusation” in BSB.
The Hebrew oath says “thus may God do” and “thus may He add”; BSB makes punishment and severity explicit.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says he could no longer answer Abner a word and leaves him unnamed; BSB names Ish-bosheth and expresses inability as not daring.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew leaves the speaker unnamed and twice uses seeing “my face”; BSB names David and first uses “appear before me.”
The Hebrew says “give” without a separate word for “back.”
The Hebrew refers to the woman as “her”; BSB supplies Michal.
The Hebrew describes her husband going with her and going on weeping behind her. His return has no explicit destination “home.”
The Hebrew uses “yesterday and the day before yesterday,” rendered “In the past” in BSB.
The Hebrew uses an infinitive for saving, without an explicit finite “I will save.” It preserves David’s hand and singular “hand” for the enemies; BSB omits the first and pluralizes the latter.
The Hebrew repeats Abner’s name and uses the images of the ears of Benjamin and David and the eyes of Israel and Benjamin; BSB expresses these without the bodily images.
The Hebrew explicitly names Abner again as a recipient of the feast; BSB uses “them.”
The Hebrew explicitly speaks of rising and uses “soul” rather than BSB’s “heart.”
The Hebrew calls the returning group David’s servants and leaves the sender of Abner unnamed; BSB uses “soldiers” and names David.
The Hebrew describes the reporting actively with unnamed plural subjects; BSB uses passive “he was informed.”
The Hebrew strengthens the going-away verb by repetition; BSB says he “is getting away.”
The Hebrew separately names going out and coming in and repeats the verb for knowing; BSB condenses these as tracking movements.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew has no separate “as if” and leaves the striker, the dying man, and Asahel’s brother unnamed in pronouns; BSB explicitly supplies Joab and Abner.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew uses singular “the head of Joab” and coordinates the house of his father; BSB says “the heads of Joab and the entire house.”
Close to the Hebrew.
